summary: Sol Health is an offline health app for an astronaut alone on a deep-space mission, where the flight surgeon is minutes away. It compares each reading with the astronaut's own normal, says whether something is wrong and why, tells them what to do, and sends what matters to Earth. It covers the indicators the challenge names (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood) plus cabin air, radiation and an eye check.
details:
Sol Health takes three kinds of input: hourly readings from a wearable (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, sleep), a short daily check-in the astronaut fills in (mood, stress, blood sugar, urine and stool results, an eye photo), and cabin sensors for CO2 and radiation.
An engine on board compares each reading with the astronaut's own normal range, learned from their earlier days. Fixed medical limits handle clear emergencies, and small statistical models watch for slow or unusual changes. It runs without an internet connection, and every alert says in one sentence what changed and by how much.



The app then shows a status of clear, watch or act now, with a short checklist. Act-now alerts reach the flight surgeon on Earth right away, and watch alerts go in a daily report. When the radiation level jumps to more than twice its weekly normal, for example, the app tells the astronaut to go to the storm shelter and alerts Earth at the same time.
We tested the engine on real data. Across five months of records from 16 people, it gave about one false alarm per person per month. It also caught the real solar storm of 20 May 2024, recorded by NASA's Curiosity rover, within its first hour.
